title: Making Tech-Industry Partnerships Work in the Agentic Era
gist: BCG reports that 90% of industrial-tech partnerships were missing their goals in 2024 and argues the failure rate will rise as agentic AI adds governance and liability strain, yet 94% of surveyed stakeholders still expect such deals to become more common. The prescription is to pick one of four partnership archetypes (AI Transformist, Tech Co-creator, Venture Launcher, Cross-Border Integrator) and pre-empt six pitfalls, with the sharpest edge being that the tech partner's exit logic is almost always to resell the industrial partner's data and know-how across the sector.

insights.claim: BCG's 2024 Tech x Industry Partnership Survey found that nine out of ten partnerships between industrial and tech companies were failing to meet their goals, based on input from 209 companies across autos, health care, and consumer plus 93 tech players.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Base rates matter: any corporate AI partnership announcement should be discounted heavily until milestones are hit, and vendors monetizing announced-but-stalled deals carry hidden revenue risk.
insights.quote: In 2024, nine out of ten partnerships between industrial and tech companies were failing to meet their goals, according to BCG research.

insights.claim: Agentic AI — autonomous systems that act, negotiate, and transact on a company's behalf — is expected to push partnership failure rates higher because it introduces governance and liability questions between firms with mismatched histories and decision speeds.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Liability and governance for autonomous agents is an unpriced friction; watch for insurers, contract-tooling, and agent-audit vendors emerging to absorb it.
insights.quote: In the era of agentic AI, when autonomous AI systems can act, negotiate, and transact on a company's behalf, the failure rate is likely to rise further.
insights.locator: In the era of agentic AI

insights.claim: Despite the poor track record, 94% of tech and industry stakeholders in BCG's survey expect tech-industry partnerships to become more common, signalling that deal volume will grow even as execution quality lags.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Rising volume against a 90% miss rate implies a growing addressable market for partnership-enablement services and consulting, not for the partnerships themselves.
insights.quote: 94% of tech and industry stakeholders said that they expected these partnerships to become more common.
insights.locator: The Strategic Value of Tech-Industry Partnerships Will Increase

insights.claim: The value in industrial AI has moved past deploying or customizing off-the-shelf tools to co-innovation, where both parties commit engineering talent, capital, and roadmap to rewire core products and workflows together.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Software vendors whose revenue is still seat-based licensing face structural pressure; those able to commit engineers and share upside capture the higher-value contracts.
insights.quote: Critically, the value unlock today is no longer about deploying or customizing off-the-shelf tools. It comes from co-innovation: both parties committing the engineering talent, capital, and roadmap required to rewire core products and workflows together.

insights.claim: Sharing of risk, governance, and upside is the dividing line between a true partnership and a vendor model in which the industrial company pays and receives a defined product or service.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A useful classification test when reading press releases: no shared governance or upside means it is a procurement contract dressed as a strategic alliance.
insights.locator: This sharing of risk, governance, and upside

insights.claim: Co-innovation drives embedded delivery, where tech-player engineers physically operate inside the industrial company to close the last mile between AI ambition and production — a model far removed from traditional tech licensing.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Embedded delivery is headcount-intensive and gross-margin dilutive for tech vendors; margin compression at AI providers may reflect this shift rather than pricing weakness.
insights.quote: tech player engineers operate inside the industrial company to close the last mile between AI ambition and production, a long way from traditional tech licensing
insights.locator: This cooperative effort drives embedded delivery

insights.claim: One three-year co-development agreement in the auto industry created a collaboration team of more than 1,400 specialists across six countries, showing the headcount scale that serious AI co-innovation now requires.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete cost anchor for modeling AI partnership spend: these are thousand-person, multi-country programs, not pilot budgets.
insights.quote: in the auto industry, one three-year co-development agreement created a collaboration team of more than 1,400 specialists across six countries
insights.locator: The new team can be quite large

insights.claim: Industrial partners bring domain-specific training data, sector knowledge, brand, and customer relationships, and act as a discipline against tokenmaxxing — measuring success in AI usage rather than revenues and margins.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Explicit warning that AI token/usage metrics are a vanity KPI; treat vendor-reported usage growth as weak evidence of customer value creation.
insights.quote: steering projects away from “interesting” technical challenges or tokenmaxxing, which measures success in AI usage rather than revenues and margins
insights.locator: A leading industrial company can supply

insights.claim: The deeper the rewiring of an industry, the harder negotiations become over governance, platform lock-in, and IP ownership — meaning the most transformative partnerships are also structurally the most likely to stall.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Ambition and completion probability are inversely related; the boldest announced alliances deserve the steepest execution discount.
insights.quote: However, rewiring an industry in this way, makes negotiations over governance, platform lock-in, and IP ownership even more difficult.
insights.locator: However, rewiring an industry in this way

themes.theme: Four Archetypes with Named Deal Precedents

insights.claim: BCG identifies four tech-industry partnership archetypes — AI Transformist, Tech Co-creator, Venture Launcher, and Cross-Border Integrator — and argues none is superior in all settings, so partners must candidly assess partially aligned goals before choosing.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A ready taxonomy for classifying any announced AI alliance and inferring which economics (services, equity, licensing, market access) actually drive it.
insights.quote: In our work with clients, we see four archetypes in common use. No archetype is superior to the others in all settings.

insights.claim: Australian life insurer TAL's strategic partnership with Microsoft produced internal AI tools including a knowledge base that TAL says saves seven minutes per question and earned 93% positive user feedback — an AI Transformist case where benefits only materialize after deep embedding.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Rare disclosed AI ROI metrics in insurance workflow; note they are time-saved and satisfaction figures, not revenue or margin, which is the standard weakness of AI case studies.
insights.quote: including a knowledge base that TAL says saves seven minutes per question and has earned 93% positive user feedback

insights.claim: Within the Tech Co-creator archetype, autos illustrates three distinct industrial roles: integrator (automaker partnerships with self-driving platform Wayve), co-developer (BMW's extensive partnership with Qualcomm to build a platform sellable to other OEMs), and lead developer (Tesla's deep relationship with Samsung for AI chips and connectivity).
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The role an OEM takes determines who owns the resellable platform IP — BMW/Qualcomm-style co-development creates a supplier product line, while Tesla-style lead development keeps value in-house.

insights.claim: Sanofi's Venture Launcher partnership with pharmatech firm Owkin to build AI agents for drug discovery involved a $180 million equity investment in Owkin stock when it started in 2021.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete price point for pharma buying an equity foothold in AI drug discovery; useful comparable when valuing private AI-bio platforms.
insights.quote: When the partnership started in 2021, Sanofi invested $180 million in Owkin stock.

insights.claim: Volkswagen's partnership with Chinese EV specialist XPeng builds EVs in China combining VW's engineering and production know-how with XPeng's advanced software platform including self-driving — the Cross-Border Integrator play for market access.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Signals that Western OEMs now source software capability from Chinese partners rather than the reverse — a reversal of the historic technology-transfer direction in China JVs.

insights.claim: Some large European companies have partnered with French AI firm Mistral specifically because they want to align with a local, European player, meaning partner selection is being made on geopolitical rather than purely technical grounds.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Sovereignty preference creates a defensible demand pocket for regional AI champions even where frontier capability lags US labs — relevant to Mistral-type valuations.
insights.quote: some large European companies have formed partnerships with the French AI firm Mistral because they want to align with a local, European player
insights.locator: In some cases, industrial companies select a partner on geopolitical grounds

themes.theme: Design-Time Pitfalls: Value Proposition, Incentives, IP

insights.claim: BCG splits the six partnership pitfalls into four design-time failures (hazy value proposition, misaligned goals and incentives, unclear data and IP ownership, unclear governance) and two execution failures (failure to activate results, failure to bridge cultures), arguing anything ill-conceived at signing is inherited by everything downstream.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Diligence checklist: most partnership value is won or lost before signature, so the contract terms — not the press release — are the leading indicator.
insights.quote: The first four are design-time pitfalls; if any provisions are ill-conceived at the agreement signing stage, everything downstream of them inherits the problem.
insights.locator: The Six Pitfalls of Tech-Industry Partnerships

insights.claim: Partnerships should be structured with near-term and interim milestones alongside a three-to-five-year vision — first-year targets building foundations and quick wins, years two and three expanding to broader use cases — because a hazy value proposition is the most common cause of high-profile alliances producing nothing.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Absence of dated interim milestones in an announced partnership is a concrete red flag for eventual quiet abandonment.
insights.quote: Every sector has seen a landmark partnership agreement between an industry giant and a global software company that generates a lot of excitement and then... nothing.

insights.claim: Industrial companies should settle internal conflicts first — the CTO pushing for scale, the CFO holding costs, business units wanting quick wins — before opening talks with the tech partner, since unresolved internal splits surface mid-negotiation and define red lines too late.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Internal misalignment is a diagnosable delay driver; slow negotiation timelines often reflect buyer-side politics rather than vendor pricing.

insights.claim: Rather than debating deal structures in the abstract, partners should quantify two or three realistic structures — for example a narrow use-case license versus a full co-development agreement — scored on speed to value, control retained, and IP exposure, so the model rather than the loudest executive picks the structure.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A transferable three-axis scoring rubric (speed to value, control, IP exposure) for evaluating any build-versus-partner AI decision.
insights.quote: This amounts to letting the model pick the structure, instead of deferring to the person in the room who argues loudest.

insights.claim: Platform lock-in can be contractually pre-empted with mandated multicloud or multimodel clauses, data-portability rights, and periodic price benchmarking against market alternatives.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: If multimodel clauses become standard enterprise practice, model-layer switching costs fall and pricing power concentrates further in infrastructure rather than models.
insights.quote: Options may include a mandated multicloud or multimodel clause, data-portability rights, and periodic price benchmarking against market alternatives.

insights.claim: In most partnerships the tech player's exit logic is to sell the data and know-how gained from the industrial partner across the rest of the sector, using that partner as a reference account — so the industrial partner should negotiate a time-limited exclusivity window against named rivals in exchange for lower ongoing fees.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The real economics of AI partnerships: the tech vendor is buying sector-wide productization rights cheaply, which compounds its moat while the first-mover industrial gets only a timing lead.
insights.quote: In most partnerships, the tech player’s exit logic involves selling data and know-how from the industry partner across the sector, using the industry partner as a reference.

insights.claim: IP negotiations should fully declare preexisting background IP, distinguish hard IP such as patents requiring formal ownership from soft IP such as NDA-protected know-how, and include termination clauses specifying IP disposition if the partnership ends.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Soft IP — know-how — is the leakiest asset in AI partnerships and the hardest to claw back at termination; check whether deals address it at all.

insights.claim: Fighting for blanket data ownership creates a win/lose dynamic that drains partnership momentum; the winnable approach is narrow carve-outs blocking use against named rivals, specific regions, and key use cases while giving the tech player a free hand elsewhere.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Implies enterprise data exclusivity will be narrow and time-boxed in practice, so AI vendors retain broad rights to generalize customer learnings across an industry.
insights.quote: the industry player should prevent the data and IP from being used where it really hurts (named rivals, specific regions, key use cases) but otherwise give the tech player a free hand
insights.locator: Conflicts over data ownership can be a trap

insights.claim: Choosing a series of narrow use-case tech partnerships lowers data risk but forfeits the industry-defining impact of a comprehensive alliance with a global software or AI player — an explicit risk-versus-impact tradeoff.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Companies fragmenting AI spend across many small vendors are implicitly accepting a lower ceiling on transformation — a way to read a customer's ambition from its procurement pattern.
insights.locator: In addition, the industry partner has options

insights.claim: Effective partnership governance is a four-layer living cadence: annual CEO review, quarterly executive sponsor meetings on KPIs and IP outputs, twice-monthly partnership leader meetings, and monthly value-stream manager meetings on blockers.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete operating template; absence of a named partnership leader and a fixed meeting cadence is a reliable early sign a deal will drift.
insights.quote: Governance is not simply a matter of writing the appropriate partnership agreement. It is a multilayer, living process

insights.claim: Good foundation work — aligned KPIs and wide ownership — paradoxically makes stakeholders more reluctant to shut down an alliance that has served its purpose, so reviews should include impartial stakeholders and be auto-triggered when key KPIs are missed.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Zombie partnerships inflate reported enterprise AI spend and vendor backlogs; sunk-cost persistence means announced deal counts overstate live economic activity.
insights.quote: companies may keep a partnership alive even when it no longer delivers value
insights.locator: Unclear governance brings an additional risk

themes.theme: Execution Pitfalls: Activation and Decision Latency

insights.claim: Partnership output dies at the business-unit level when units have different priorities, lack agentic AI skills, or have no incentive to deploy IP that originated outside their domain — the fix is aligning BU KPIs to partnership IP use and creating a dedicated partnership office.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Explains the pilot-to-production gap in enterprise AI: the constraint is incentive design inside the buyer, not model capability.
insights.quote: If the front line does not see a path to revenue, the whole thing fizzles out.

insights.claim: The real tech-industry fault line is not cultural mismatch but decision latency: the tech player decides in days while the industrial partner needs an approval process measured in weeks.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Reframes a soft 'culture' problem into a measurable cycle-time metric that can be diligenced and fixed with delegated mandates.
insights.quote: Despite frequent talk of cultural mismatches, the real issue is the speed of decision making. The tech player decides in days; the industrial partner needs to complete an approval process measured in weeks.

insights.claim: Latency mismatch is best resolved by the industrial side using pilots that require fewer approvals, sandboxes that reduce technical risk and therefore sign-offs, and a speed boat structure with a pre-delegated decision mandate and budget so the partnership lead never re-enters the mothership approval chain.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Practical structure to look for in enterprise AI programs; deals routed through standard corporate approval chains will underperform carved-out ones.
insights.quote: One possible model is the speed boat methodology, which allows the partnership to accelerate away from the slow-moving mothership.
insights.locator: Structure the partnership to decouple from business as usual

themes.theme: Where AI Shifts the Profit Pools

insights.claim: AI being woven into the core fabric of every product and workflow will change which parts of the value chain capture the most significant profit, making partnership choice a determinant of future profit-pool position rather than a procurement decision.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Frames AI as a profit-pool reallocation event within industries — the trade is identifying which layer of each value chain captures the rent, not whether AI is adopted.
insights.quote: Increasingly, AI will be woven into the core fabric of every product and workflow, changing the parts of the value chain that capture the most significant profit.
insights.locator: The Strategic Value of Tech-Industry Partnerships Will Increase

insights.claim: Because the tech player will probably eventually sell the jointly developed IP to the wider market, the industrial partner's durable advantage is shaping that IP from the start and getting access potentially years ahead of rivals — valuable given the time-compounding nature of AI development.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The payoff from AI partnerships is a timing lead that compounds, not permanent exclusivity — supports early-mover premiums even where the technology later commoditizes.
insights.quote: the company will gain access potentially years ahead of its rivals, a vital competitive advantage given the time-compounding nature of AI development
insights.locator: Although the tech player will probably eventually offer the IP

insights.claim: The greater risk for an industrial company is not a failed partnership but proceeding without a plan on the assumption that tech magic sprinkled on existing products and services will future-proof the business.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Sets the bar for management quality: incumbents announcing AI without an archetype, milestones, or IP terms are signalling superficial engagement.
insights.quote: the bigger risk for the industrial partner would be to proceed without a plan, thinking that tech magic sprinkled on their products and services will future-proof their business
